newsitem.title: CHINA: China cremates paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
newsitem.headline: China cremates paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.

text.p: China cremated paramount leader Deng Xiaoping on Monday after his successor President Jiang Zemin and the elite of the ruling Communist Party bowed before the body of the man who transformed the nation.
Deng had lain in state surrounded by flowers and cypress branches in the 301 military hospital before making his last journey to the Babaoshan cemetery, the Xinhua news agency said.
"Eternal Glory to Comrade Deng Xiaoping," read a streamer above his body in the hospital where his body has lain since he died last Wednesday, aged 92.

His designated heir Jiang, Premier Li Peng, the five other members of the all-powerful Politburo and several other leaders, wearing black armbands and with a white paper flower of mourning in their buttonholes, bowed three times before the body.

A white van bedecked with black and yellow ribbons, the colours of mourning, carried Deng's body at a stately pace to the cemetery in western Beijing where Chinese communism's heroes are traditionally laid to rest.
"Scatter Hot Tears for Comrade Xiaoping," read a banner with black characters held up by one group of people.
"Go gently, Xiaoping," read another.

Hundreds of armed police, a fraction of the huge security force activated as China treads warily along the road of political transition, lined streets along the 2.5-km (1.5-mile) route to the cemetery.

The cortege moved at a pace allowing thousands of mourners lining the route a last glimpse of the man who ruled China for 18 years with a blend of capitalist-style economic policies and communist political control.
"I have come to say goodbye to Deng Xiaoping," said a young man.
As the cavalcade passed, people stood on roofs of buildings or climbed up lamp posts for a better view.
But some residents did not know Deng's body was to be moved and were upset that their routine had been disrupted.
"Hey, move it, some of us have to go to work," grumbled one middle-aged woman pushing her bicycle through the crowd.
Outside Babaoshan stood hundreds of workers bussed in from from the nearby steel works.
One manager of the giant state-run enterprise, Yue Wenhui, 44, asked why he was willing to wait outside on a wintry day, said: "The weather is good. It is as misty as our hearts."
After the cremation, the ashes were expected to be taken to the cavernous Great Hall of the People on Tiananmen Square.
Deng, an opponent of the leadership cult around his predecessor Mao Zedong, made clear he wanted more restrained mourning than the near-hysteria that followed Mao's demise in 1976.
No foreign dignitaries have been invited to Tuesday's rites in the Great Hall. Deng's ashes will be scattered at sea.
Deng's family requested that his body not be put on display, that his corneas be donated to an eye bank and his body offered for medical dissection before cremation.
China has sought to project stability and continuity in the aftermath of Deng's death, painfully aware of the tumult that has often followed the death of strongmen throughout China's history.

Since his death authorities have heightened their security watch around the capital and especially in Tiananmen Square, the vast central space where, in 1989, student-led protests were crushed by troops and tanks at Deng's behest.
